analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run single-payer health program covering everyone, funded by higher taxes on income, payroll, corporations, tobacco, and alcohol.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single Democratic senator with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based insurance with a national health program run by the states under federal rules. Every resident would be enrolled automatically and get comprehensive care — including dental, vision, mental health, prescription drugs, and long-term care — with no coverage denied for preexisting conditions. It would be paid for by raising income tax rates, adding a new payroll tax, raising corporate taxes, and sharply increasing excise taxes on cigarettes, beer, wine, and liquor. Private insurance that duplicates the public plan would be banned.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen and legal resident would gain guaranteed, portable coverage regardless of health condition, income, or where they live [S2][S3]. People who are uninsured, underinsured, denied for preexisting conditions, or burdened by premiums, deductibles, and surprise bills would benefit most [S2]. The bill also directs extra resources to rural areas and health-professional shortage areas and bars discrimination in services [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone, especially the uninsured and underinsured

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a single-payer national health program, administered by states under federal guidelines, covering every citizen and lawful resident regardless of health condition, income, or location [S2][S3].

Covers all medically necessary services including hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, hearing, vision, mental health, substance abuse treatment, hospice, and long-term care, and prohibits states from limiting covered services because of preexisting conditions [S2][S3].
Enrolls people automatically at birth or immigration and lets coverage travel across state lines, with no residence waiting period beyond three months [S2][S3].
Providers accepting program payment must take it as payment in full, eliminating balance billing, and private insurance duplicating covered services is prohibited [S2][S3].

Finances the program progressively through higher individual and corporate income tax rates, a new uncapped payroll tax on employees (1.45%) and employers (7.45%), and higher excise taxes on tobacco and alcohol, deposited in a National Health Care Trust Fund [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally, through income tax rate increases (the 15% rate rising to 20%, the 28% to 31%, the 31% to 39%), a new uncapped payroll tax split between employees and employers, a corporate rate increase from 34% to 39%, and higher taxes on Social Security benefits [S2][S3]. Smokers and drinkers would pay sharply higher excise taxes — cigarette taxes roughly doubling and beer taxes more than quadrupling [S3]. Employers would swap health premiums for a 7.45% payroll tax on all wages [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, employers, and tobacco and alcohol users

drawbacks.text: The tax burden is substantial and broad: individual income tax rates rise across the board, the corporate rate jumps from 34% to 39%, and an uncapped combined 8.9% payroll tax falls on every dollar of wages and self-employment income [S2][S3].
It repeals Medicare and Medicaid outright and folds them into the new program, so tens of millions of beneficiaries would depend entirely on a successful transition to a brand-new system [S2][S3].
Private insurance that duplicates covered services is banned, eliminating the option of buying supplementary coverage for care the public plan already covers [S2][S3].

National spending is capped at prior-year spending plus the growth in gross national product, and states must limit acquisition of expensive specialized equipment and impose cost-sharing for some services, which critics could argue constrains access to advanced care [S2][S3].
Every state must contribute its own funding, and no individual is eligible unless their state makes required payments — giving states leverage to underfund or delay the program [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered the largest possible version of health reform: universal comprehensive coverage, including benefits like long-term care and dental care that most plans then and now exclude, financed by visibly progressive taxes. The honest trade-offs are real — a large and broadly distributed tax increase, a ban on duplicative private coverage, hard spending caps tied to economic growth, and the risk of replacing Medicare and Medicaid before the replacement system is proven. Whether the trade was worth making is a legitimate political question; what is not disputed is that the bill never came close to being tested — it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Inouye introduced the National Health Care Act of 1992 in the Senate on June 9, 1992 [S1][S5].
No senator from either party cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — was ever recorded [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and all pending bills died [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry kept its market for covering care, employers kept the premium-based system, and the status quo of tens of millions uninsured continued. In 1992 the uninsured population stood near 37 million, and no reform passed in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The insurance industry and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Daniel K. Inouye
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Care Act of 1992 and became its only sponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers whose core business of covering health care would be replaced for covered services
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against single-payer proposals during the early-1990s health reform debate, contributing to a climate in which no such bill advanced

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so it never developed a partisan profile; it simply had no support beyond its author [S4].

industries.note: The bill prohibits selling private insurance that duplicates covered services and repeals employer-based coverage, wiping out the industry's core market overnight; it could sell only policies for services the public plan excludes. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the public's interest in universal coverage.

Providers would get guaranteed payment from a single payer covering everyone, with subsidies for rural and shortage-area facilities, but would have to accept program payment as payment in full, operate under negotiated global budgets and fee schedules, and give up control over capital purchases and balance billing.

Employers would stop paying private health premiums and their retiree coverage obligations would be replaced by a tax, but they would owe a new uncapped 7.45% payroll tax on every wage, a heavier burden for firms with large payrolls than premiums they currently dodge.

Excise taxes rise steeply — beer from $18 to $81 a barrel, cigarettes from $12 to $20 per thousand, distilled spirits from $13.50 to $29 per proof gallon — plus one-time floor-stocks taxes, costs that largely pass through to consumers who smoke and drink.

Top income tax rates rise, the estate and trust tax rates increase, the share of Social Security benefits subject to income tax goes up with lower thresholds, and the new payroll tax has no wage cap — so high earners bear the largest dollar increases while receiving the same universal coverage.
